final_answer:
Bottom line: the husband's best route is a motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia removal order before the immigration court based on lack of notice (INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii); 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii)). It may be filed at any time, automatically stays removal, and (as of April 1, 2026) carries no filing fee, including no H.R. 1 fee. If granted, he can pursue adjustment of status in removal proceedings.

1. What to file with the immigration court. A motion to reopen and rescind the in absentia order, filed with the immigration court that entered the order (not the BIA), with a proposed cover page, supporting declaration(s), and evidence that he did not receive notice 'in accordance with' INA 239(a)(1) or (2). The facts help: USCIS mailed the NTA to an address he never gave, the same wrong address that caused the missed RFE. Evidence should include his declaration, proof of his actual address (USCIS filings showing the correct address on the I-130/I-485, lease, etc.), the RFE/denial envelopes showing the wrong address, the NTA, and the FOIA/ROP record showing the mailing address. Request rescission, termination or a new hearing, and state the relief he will seek. Also file an EOIR-33 change of address with the court once the case is reopened or as the Practice Manual directs. Under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) such a motion has no deadline, and filing it automatically stays removal (INA 240(b)(5)(C)). Caution: Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024) holds the alien must show he lacked notice under both paragraph (1) and (2) of 239(a); if the court mailed a hearing notice to the address of record and he was bound to provide an address, the court may find notice proper. Here, if the only address ever used was one he never provided and DHS never received a correct address in the proceeding, he can argue no valid notice (note the proper-address / duty-to-provide-address issue, 239(a)(1)(F), 239(a)(2)(B)/(c), must be addressed; if he was never served and thus never told of his address obligation, the no-notice argument is strong). A fallback motion based on exceptional circumstances must be filed within 180 days of the order (August 1, 2025 + 180 days has passed by April 1, 2026), so lack of notice is the only practical ground; an alternative is requesting sua sponte reopening (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(1)), which is discretionary.

2. Fees. For lack-of-notice motions to reopen an in absentia order there is no fee; the $145 regulatory fee plus $900 H.R. 1 (OBBBA) fee ($1,045 total) applies to other in absentia motions (e.g., exceptional circumstances) but not to the statutory lack-of-notice or custody motions (EOIR PM 25-36, July 17, 2025, per secondary summaries I reviewed; I did not independently open the memo). Fee waivers for IJ motions are not available for the H.R. 1 fee. If the order is rescinded and he renews adjustment before the IJ, USCIS filing fees may apply (I-485 and a new I-130 if needed) under USCIS's current fee schedule; I did not verify the amounts.

3. The I-130 and I-485 denials. (a) USCIS motion: a motion to reopen/reconsider on Form I-290B is due within 30 days (33 if mailed) of the decision, but 8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i) lets USCIS excuse lateness where the delay was reasonable and beyond the applicant's control; the failure to receive the RFE because of USCIS's own misaddress supports that, though the long delay (denials Dec 2023/Jan 2024; discovery April 2026) and discretionary nature make it uncertain. The 'no response to RFE' denial may also be challenged as an error if USCIS did not mail to the address of record. (b) No appeal lies from an I-485 denial, but a non-arriving applicant may renew the application before an immigration judge in removal proceedings (8 CFR 245.2(a)(5)(ii); 1245.2(a)(5)(ii)). Because the husband was admitted on a B-2 visa and is an immediate relative of a US citizen, INA 245(c) bars (overstay, unauthorized employment) do not apply, so renewed adjustment is viable once proceedings are reopened. The IJ cannot adjudicate an I-130; a new (or reopened) I-130 must go to USCIS, and the IJ may continue the case for it (a prima facie approvable petition is needed). The I-130 and I-485 would be required to be refiled or the I-485 renewed with a fresh I-130 and supporting Form I-864 etc.

4. Risks. Marriage 19 days after entry on a B-2 visa invites a preconceived-intent / misrepresentation (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i)) inquiry and a bona fide marriage review under INA 204(c)/245; the couple should assemble robust bona fide marriage evidence. If the order stays and he is removed, he faces a 10-year bar only if he departs after accruing more than a year of unlawful presence (he accrued over a year after June 1, 2023, so departure would trigger the 10-year bar of INA 212(a)(9)(B)); note an in absentia order also carries a 10-year bar to relief (INA 240(b)(7)) unless rescinded, which is why rescission is critical. Consult counsel promptly; also consider federal court review (petition for review within 30 days of an order denying the motion, INA 242(b)(1)).

Caveats: I did not fully verify every figure; consult current EOIR Practice Manual and fee schedule.
